title: "Monte Carlo integration"

The passage-contrast target (PCT) has no convenient closed-form posterior. Monte Carlo integration replaces an expectation under that posterior with an average over draws while keeping posterior uncertainty distinct from numerical error.

## Expectations as integrals

For a target density $f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)$ and an integrable function $g$,

$$
I
=
\mathbb{E}[g(\eta)\mid\mathbf y]
=
\int g(\eta)f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)\,\mathrm d\eta.
$$

Independent target draws give the estimator

$$
\widehat I_S
=
\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^Sg(\eta^{(s)}).
$$

Setting $g(\eta)=\mu$ estimates the posterior mean of the passage location. Setting $g(\eta)=\mathbf 1\{\mu>0\}$ estimates its directional probability, while $g(\eta)=\exp(\mu)$ gives a central geometric-scale noun-to-verb ratio.

## Drawing from the PCT grid

The code below reconstructs the PCT from the 55 passage summaries, normalizes its $321\times321$ reference grid, and samples 20,000 grid cells with their posterior weights.

```{r}
#| label: provo-grid-monte-carlo
provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
y <- provo$noun_minus_verb_log_ffd
N <- length(y)
nu <- 4
prior_scale <- 2 * sd(y)

log_sum_exp <- function(x) {
  maximum <- max(x)
  maximum + log(sum(exp(x - maximum)))
}

log_posterior_eta <- function(eta) {
  mu <- eta[1]
  sigma <- exp(eta[2])
  sum(dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = nu, log = TRUE) - log(sigma)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) +
    log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) + eta[2]
}

mode_fit <- optim(
  c(median(y), log(mad(y))),
  function(eta) -log_posterior_eta(eta),
  method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000L)
)
local_sd <- sqrt(diag(solve(mode_fit$hessian)))
mu_grid <- seq(mode_fit$par[1] - 7 * local_sd[1],
               mode_fit$par[1] + 7 * local_sd[1], length.out = 321L)
log_sigma_grid <- seq(mode_fit$par[2] - 7 * local_sd[2],
                      mode_fit$par[2] + 7 * local_sd[2], length.out = 321L)
grid <- expand.grid(mu = mu_grid, log_sigma = log_sigma_grid)
grid$log_kernel <- apply(grid, 1, log_posterior_eta)
grid$weight <- exp(grid$log_kernel - log_sum_exp(grid$log_kernel))

set.seed(2026101802)
S <- 20000L
draw_indices <- sample(seq_len(nrow(grid)), S, replace = TRUE,
                       prob = grid$weight)
draws <- grid[draw_indices, ]

quadrature <- c(
  mean_mu = sum(grid$mu * grid$weight),
  probability_mu_positive = sum(grid$weight[grid$mu > 0]),
  mean_exp_mu = sum(exp(grid$mu) * grid$weight)
)
estimate <- c(
  mean(draws$mu), mean(draws$mu > 0), mean(exp(draws$mu))
)
mcse <- c(
  sd(draws$mu) / sqrt(S),
  sqrt(estimate[2] * (1 - estimate[2]) / S),
  sd(exp(draws$mu)) / sqrt(S)
)

stopifnot(N == 55L, abs(sum(grid$weight) - 1) < 1e-12)
data.frame(functional = names(quadrature), quadrature, estimate, mcse)
```

The grid benchmark and Monte Carlo estimates agree to the scale of their Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSEs). For independent draws,

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\widehat I_S)
=
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(g(\eta))}{S}}.
$$

For an indicator this becomes

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}
=
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat I_S(1-\widehat I_S)}{S}}.
$$

Multiplying $S$ by four tends to halve MCSE. This square-root rate concerns the approximation, not the posterior spread.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-monte-carlo-running
#| fig-cap: "Running Monte Carlo estimate of the PCT directional probability. The horizontal line is the quadrature reference."
library(ggplot2)
running <- cumsum(draws$mu > 0) / seq_len(S)
display_index <- unique(round(seq(10, S, length.out = 600L)))
running_display <- data.frame(
  draws = display_index,
  estimate = running[display_index]
)

ggplot(running_display, aes(draws, estimate)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey35", linewidth = 0.65) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = quadrature[2], color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Independent grid draws",
       y = "Estimated posterior probability that mu > 0") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The law of large numbers justifies convergence of the average when the expectation exists. A central limit theorem motivates MCSE when $g(\eta)$ has finite variance. Neither result says that the PCT's passage aggregation, likelihood, or empirically calibrated priors are adequate.

## Two uncertainties

Posterior spread describes model-based uncertainty about the PCT. Monte Carlo error describes finite numerical approximation. Increasing $S$ reduces the latter but adds no passages, positions, or readers. More draws are not more linguistic evidence.

## Check your understanding

1. Which function $g$ estimates $\mathbb{P}(\mu>0\mid\mathbf y)$?
2. Why is the estimate an integral approximation?
3. What happens to MCSE when $S$ is quadrupled?
4. Which uncertainty requires additional linguistic observations to change?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Use the indicator $g(\eta)=\mathbf 1\{\mu>0\}$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The sample average replaces the posterior integral of $g(\eta)$ with an empirical average over draws from that posterior. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Quadrupling $S$ tends to halve MCSE because MCSE decreases at the $1/\sqrt S$ rate. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Posterior uncertainty about the linguistic target changes with additional linguistic observations; more simulation draws change only computational uncertainty. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
